terms.grammar: with the nominative or a clause (in comedy also the accusative)
evidence: Plaut. Most. 382: Ecce autem iterum hīc dēposīvit caput et dormit.
Cic. Att. 2.8.1: ecce tibi nūntius puerōs vēnisse Rōmā!
terms.comment: The everyday word. Ecce autem, “but look!”, brings in a surprise in a story; ecce tibi with a clause is the letters’ “and what do you know”; ecce mē, “here I am” (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: with the nominative or the accusative
terms.register: mostly in Vergil (Lewis & Short); in Plaut. and Ter. usually written em
terms.comment: Livelier than ecce, often indignant: ēn habet vim indignātiōnis (Donatus, quoted by Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: look, here he is! here she is!
terms.grammar: from ecce eum, ecce eam; also eccōs, eccās
evidence: Plaut. Stich. 577: atque eccum tibi lupum in sermōne

phrases.latin: Ecce autem iterum hīc dēposīvit caput et dormit. suscitā.
phrases.english: Look, he’s put his head down again and is asleep. Wake him.

phrases.latin: ecce autem geminī ā Tenedō tranquilla per alta (horrēscō referēns) immēnsīs orbibus anguēs incumbunt pelagō
phrases.english: but look! two serpents from Tenedos, over the calm deep (I shudder to tell it), lean on the sea in huge coils

phrases.latin: ecce tibi nūntius puerōs vēnisse Rōmā!
phrases.english: and what do you know, word that the boys have come from Rome!
Oh! look, there he is himself.
